analysis.one_liner: Funds naloxone distribution, addiction treatment, recovery services, and stronger insurance parity enforcement to fight the opioid crisis.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a House floor vote before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill was a broad response to the heroin and prescription opioid crisis. It would fund programs to buy and distribute naloxone, the drug that reverses overdoses, expand syringe exchange programs, and pay for treatment and recovery services, including for pregnant women and adolescents. It would also let more health professionals prescribe buprenorphine, a medication for opioid addiction, and force health insurers to prove they are covering mental health and addiction care on equal terms with other medical care. It died without any committee or floor action.
analysis.who_benefits: People with opioid addiction, people at risk of overdose, pregnant and postpartum women with substance use disorders, adolescents needing treatment, young people in recovery, and families and communities hit hard by the epidemic. Health professionals treating addiction would also gain, through new grant funding and a loan repayment program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with opioid addiction and their families

how_it_helps.text: Establishes grant programs to encourage doctors to co-prescribe naloxone, the overdose reversal drug, and to offset copays so cost is not a barrier for patients.
Authorizes $20 million a year in grants to purchase and distribute naloxone and train first responders, and $15 million a year to support syringe exchange programs.

Authorizes $300 million a year in grants to expand medication-assisted treatment and evidence-based counseling in areas with high or rapidly rising opioid use, distributed across rural, urban, and suburban areas.

Raises the limit on how many patients a doctor can treat with buprenorphine from 30 to 100, and lets nurse practitioners and physician assistants prescribe it after 24 hours of training, greatly expanding access to addiction medication.
Reauthorizes residential treatment programs for pregnant and postpartum women at $40 million a year and creates grants for adolescent treatment and recovery services at $25 million a year.

Strengthens enforcement of the law requiring health plans to cover mental health and addiction benefits on par with medical and surgical benefits, through mandatory disclosures, randomized audits, public reporting of denial rates, and a consumer complaint portal.

Authorizes $100 million a year for recovery support services, $30 million a year for a youth recovery initiative including recovery high schools, and a loan repayment program of up to $35,000 a year for addiction treatment professionals serving shortage areas.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund new programs authorized at more than $500 million a year. Opioid prescribers would pay a new training requirement, covered through their own federal licensing fees. Health insurers and group health plans would bear the cost of parity audits, disclosure reports, and covering addiction and mental health claims they may currently restrict.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, opioid prescribers, and health insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes roughly $560 million a year in new federal spending across its grant programs, a real cost to taxpayers even if much of it flows to services with proven demand.

Every practitioner registered to prescribe opioids for pain would have to complete at least 12 hours of training every three years, funded through prescriber licensing fees, a burden that could fall hardest on small practices and rural prescribers already stretched thin.

Expanding buprenorphine access, by raising the patient cap from 30 to 100 and authorizing nurse practitioners and physician assistants to prescribe, raises the possibility of increased diversion of the medication; the bill itself directs a government evaluation covering changes in treatment availability and diversion of addiction treatment medication.
Naloxone purchase grants could channel public money toward high-priced brand-name overdose reversal products rather than cheaper generic alternatives, raising program costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits target a crisis that was killing tens of thousands of Americans a year, and its costs are mostly ordinary federal grant spending. The strongest objections are the new training mandate for prescribers and the risk of buprenorphine diversion, but the bill builds in evaluations of both. On balance, the help it would offer far outweighs the costs, which is what makes its quiet death notable.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to four committees, which in turn sent it to several subcommittees, and none of them ever took it up before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017, so it received no vote of any kind.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. introduced the bill on January 28, 2016.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce Committees on the day of introduction.
Between January and March 2016 it was referred to seven subcommittees, including Health, Crime, and three education and workforce subcommittees, splitting it among many panels.
No committee ever reported the bill, and the full action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor action after the March 2016 subcommittee referrals.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, so the bill died without a vote in either chamber.
The bill had 34 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors listed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and group health plans came out ahead, since the parity audits, disclosure requirements, and public denial-rate reporting they would have faced never became law. Prescribers also avoided the new training requirement, and no new federal spending was authorized. Communities hit by the opioid epidemic received nothing from this bill, though Congress did enact other opioid legislation that year.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and group health plans

sides.party_line_note: All 34 cosponsors were Democrats, no Republican cosponsor appears in the record, and no committee or floor vote ever occurred, so no record of opposition votes exists.

industries.industry: Substance use disorder treatment and recovery providers
industries.note: The bill directs large annual grants, more than $500 million a year in total across programs, toward treatment, recovery, and prevention services, with providers and state agencies as recipients. Their gain comes from delivering services to people the epidemic has left underserved.

industries.industry: Health insurers and group health plans
industries.note: The bill would require plans to disclose how they apply non-quantitative treatment limits to mental health and addiction benefits, submit to randomized federal audits, and have their claim denial rates published on a public portal. Their financial interest in restricting addiction coverage runs against the bill's aim of enforcing equal coverage.

industries.industry: Naloxone and overdose reversal drug manufacturers
industries.note: Grant programs would fund purchases of naloxone and offset patient copays, creating new demand for these products. The drugs save lives, so the industry's gain runs alongside the public's, though the bill does nothing to constrain prices.

industries.industry: Opioid prescribers (physicians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants)
industries.note: They would face a new 12-hour training requirement funded by their own licensing fees, but also gain expanded authority: a buprenorphine patient cap raised from 30 to 100 and, for nurse practitioners and physician assistants, the ability to prescribe it for the first time.
